account: Thorn's chief executive, Julie Cordua, recounted the case at an Amazon conference in Las Vegas, and WIRED's Tom Simonite quoted her on 19 June 2019. The source places the case in April 2019 without a day. Cordua said that a California law enforcement officer had screenshotted a missing child's picture from a post by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The officer ran it through Spotlight, Thorn's investigator tool that matches faces and other clues in online sex ads. Using Amazon's facial recognition, Spotlight returned a list of ads featuring the girl, who had been sold for weeks. More traditional police work followed, and Cordua said that the child was recovered within weeks. No police or court record of this case is among the sources. Snopes had reported on 4 September 2018 that Thorn's 2017 impact report claimed that its tools helped identify 5,791 child victims and rescue 103. Snopes notes that the figures come from Thorn's surveys of police users. It also notes that viral claims conflated identification with rescue. On 10 May 2024 Thorn announced that it was moving Spotlight to a new home led by its former Vice President of Victim Identification, Kristin Boorse. Canary NGO Ltd now builds the tool and says that more than 8,000 investigators use it.

ai_role.statement: The face match that surfaced the ads is attributed to Amazon Rekognition inside Spotlight. The recovery itself came from conventional police work. Everything about this case rests on Thorn's CEO. Snopes documents that Thorn's aggregate figures derive from user surveys and were widely misreported.
